title: Replace a failed gas strut on a hinged lid: unclip it, fit the new one, check the lid holds open, close it
instruction: Replace the tagged gas strut with the new one, check that the lid holds itself open, then close the lid.
context: A gas strut that has lost its gas lets a machine lid or guard drop on the hands. Replacing it is routine work for general maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, 1,621,800 in the US), whose work includes installing machine or equipment replacement parts. Each end of a strut is a ball socket held on its ball stud by a spring clip: the clip is drawn partly out to release the socket, and the new socket is pressed on until it snaps. The lid's weight closes it until both struts work (one good strut cannot hold it), so one hand holds the lid open while the other fits the new strut, rod end down as makers recommend. The fitter then checks that the lid holds itself open, pushes it down past its balance point to close it, and an inspector tugs each new socket and lifts the lid to its stop.
setup:
Frame: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top; cm. One fixed layout (seed 0, no jitter), as in the screenshot.
- Enclosure: grey powder-coated steel box, x 18 to 38, y -20 to +20, 8 tall, 0.15 walls, fixed to the table. Its hinge side faces the robot.
- Lid: blue 0.25 cm aluminium plate 20 x 40 with 1.8 cm side flanges turned down outside the side walls, 0.63 kg. Piano hinge along the front top edge (x 18, z 8); it opens upward, away from the robot, to a stop at 45 degrees. It starts shut.
- Handle: black 1.2 cm aluminium tube 30 long (y -15 to +15), 3 proud of the lid on two posts, 18 from the hinge.
- Ball studs (4, zinc-plated steel): 0.8 cm ball on a 0.4 cm neck, ball centre 3.5 out from the face. Body studs on the outer face of each side wall at x 28.8, z 4.5 (y +-23.5). Lid studs on the outer face of each lid flange, 3.75 from the hinge along the lid and 1 below its top (lid shut: x 21.75, z 7; at its stop: x 21.4, z 9.9).
- Gas struts (3): ACE GS-10-30 class, 3 cm stroke, 9.2 cm between ball centres fully extended, black 1 cm steel body, 0.3 cm bright steel rod, 66 g. Each end is a 1.3 cm zinc-plated steel ball socket (G3.5) whose spring clip has two flat steel finger loops (1.6 x 0.6 x 0.25 cm) running on past the socket's outer end.
  - Right strut: good (10 N extension force), fitted, rod end on the body stud, compressed with the lid shut.
  - Left strut: failed (no gas force), fitted the same way, with a red defect tag (3 x 2 cm card) on its body.
  - New strut: good, fully extended, lying across the battens along x, rod end away from the robot, centred at x 9.5, y +14, socket mouths facing -y (as they face the left wall once fitted), finger loops up.
- Battens (2): plain wood, 2 x 2, 36 long along y (y -18 to +18), on the table at x 4.9 and x 14.1.
Fitted correctly, a strut runs from its body stud (rod end, low) up toward the robot to its lid stud. At the 45 degree stop the lid's weight is 0.46 N m about the hinge; one good strut gives 0.36 N m, two give 0.71 N m.
scoring:
A socket is on when its ball's centre is within 1 mm of the socket's centre and its clip is within 0.4 mm of shut. A socket counts only on its own stud (rod end on the body stud, body end on the lid stud). Highest rung reached; each rung needs the ones below; 0.15 to 0.45 are read at the end, 0.60 to 1.0 are events that, once reached, stay reached:
- 0.15: the tagged strut is off all studs and lying on the table or battens (both socket centres 3.5 cm or less above the table, not over the enclosure, no gripper within 3 cm of them).
- 0.30: and the new strut is on at one end on the left.
- 0.45: and on at both ends there.
- 0.60: and, with the new strut on at both ends and both grippers 3 cm or more from the lid, handle and struts and still for 1 s, the lid stayed at 43 degrees or more for 2 s.
- 0.80: and after that the lid was closed: within 3 degrees of shut with the grippers clear and still for 1 s.
- 1.0: and after that the inspection passed, applied by the task file while the grippers stay clear: each socket of the new strut pulled outward along its stud at 30 N for 1 s moves under 1 mm and stays on; then the lid, lifted by a force of at most 8 N on the handle to 44 degrees and let go, stays at 43 degrees or more for 2 s.
- 0 otherwise. A gripper coming back within 3 cm stops a check in progress; it starts again when the conditions hold again. The 30 N pull and the 8 N lift are this task's own test values. Real world: protractor on the hinge, 50 N spring scale with a ruler, a hand on the handle, video.
reset_notes: Refit the tagged strut (rod end down) and lay the new strut back on the battens; the clips are reusable.
fidelity: Struts at GS-10-30 size and force (10 N) as sprung, damped sliders; the failed one has no force and 5 N s/m damping; 66 g is ours. Each socket's spring clip is two sprung jaws with flat finger loops: pushing the loops outboard (about 3 N) opens it, as prying the real clip does. No maker gives a push-on force: it snaps at about 1.4 N. The strut body has a 4 mm torsional contact patch. Lid and stud sizes are ours. The task file applies the inspection.
